title: Towards a public-facing version of the CanRisk tool: Co-designing, developing and evaluating MyCanRisk.
abstract: The CanRisk tool allows healthcare professionals to calculate validated multifactorial estimates of breast, ovarian, and prostate cancer risk. To support patient involvement in risk assessment, we co-designed a public-facing tool, MyCanRisk, which allows patients to collect and share risk information in advance of a clinical appointment, without generating risk estimates. This study describes the user-centred development of MyCanRisk and its initial evaluation. Development involved co-design workshops with patients, public contributors, healthcare professionals, and researchers, followed by iterative accessibility and usability testing against WCAG 2.2. Evaluation used a multi-methods design: 51 women with a family history of breast cancer completed MyCanRisk and, approximately two weeks later, a structured clinical-style interview. Agreement in risk categorisation was assessed using Cohen's kappa. Semi-structured interviews with a purposive subsample (n=15) explored user experiences. MyCanRisk was perceived as accessible and easy to use. Agreement between MyCanRisk and structured interviews for risk categorisation was substantial (κ = 0.81, 95% CI 0.65-0.97). Discrepancies mainly reflected difficulties recalling detailed family history, such as ages at diagnosis and dates of birth/death. Participants valued the stepwise flow and asynchronous completion but reported challenges when their knowledge was incomplete. Suggested improvements included options to record approximate or unknown data and greater flexibility to update submissions. MyCanRisk has the potential to reduce data collection burden during clinical encounters, support patient preparation for risk assessment, and streamline cancer risk assessment pathways. With further refinement and testing in more diverse populations, it may facilitate earlier identification of individuals at increased cancer risk.

title: Spike gene evolution in HCoV-OC43: Evidence of post-pandemic selective expansion.
abstract: The aim is to characterise the evolution of the HCoV-OC43 spike from 2014 to 2024, spanning both the pre- and post-SARS-CoV-2 pandemic periods, in cases attended at a tertiary hospital in Catalonia. Respiratory specimens from patients with suspected acute respiratory infection were collected for laboratory-confirmation using a real-time PCR assay. A random selection of HCoV-OC43-positive specimens was performed per week. The whole spike gene was amplified by a nested RT-PCR using primers and protocol optimised from Gorse et al., 2017 and subsequently sequenced with the Illumina DNA Prep protocol. Further analyses were performed with MEGA and Nextclade softwares. The overall prevalence of seasonal coronaviruses was 5.18%, with HCoV-OC43 accounting for 47.93%. Phylogenetic analysis of the S gene revealed the predominance of cluster C. Mutation analysis showed that the RBD accumulated the highest number of substitutions prior to the pandemic, followed by a reduction afterwards, suggesting shifts in selective pressures. Positive Tajima's D values in the pre-pandemic period were consistent with stable endemic circulation, whereas negative values in the post-pandemic period suggested population expansion following a bottleneck. Comparative analyses revealed that HCoV-OC43 also exhibited lower evolutionary rates than SARS-CoV-2, in the S1 and the RBD regions, underscoring differential immune pressures. The present findings highlight the dynamic interplay between viral evolution and epidemiological changes associated with the pre- and post-pandemic periods in shaping the genetic landscape of endemic HCoVs.
journal: Enfermedades infecciosas y microbiologia clinica (English ed.)

title: Molecular epidemiological characteristics and recent trend of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) in northern Japan: the shift of major clonal group to CC1-IV (ST1/ST2725, spa-t1784) and occurrence of various novel MRSA clones.
abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major cause of infectious diseases. We analyzed the recent trends in molecular epidemiology of MRSA in northern Japan. MRSA isolates from all types of clinical specimens were genetically classified by MLST and typing schemes of SCCmec, spa, coa, and agr. Antimicrobial susceptibility was measured by broth microdilution test, and resistance/virulence determinants were detected by multiplex/uniplex PCR, and sequencing as required. A total of 321 MRSA isolates were collected during the 6-month period in 2025, and differentiated into three major clonal groups, clonal complex 1-SCCmec IV (CC1-IV)-coa-VIIa (62%), CC5-II-coa-IIa (27%), and CC8-IV-coa-IIIa (6%). The proportion of CC1-IV in 2025 increased significantly compared with that in 2011-2014 (<10%), associated with the decrease in CC5-II, while CC8-IV showed persistently low prevalence. CC1 isolates comprised a predominant ST1 and minor ST2725 and ST2764, with dominant spa-type t1784. Most CC5 MRSA consisted of ST5 (64%) and ST764 (35%), with half of ST764 isolates carrying arginine catabolic mobile element (ACME) type II'. Panton-Valentine leukocidine (PVL) genes were detected in ST8-IVa/spa-t008 with ACME-I (USA300 clone), ST22-IV with tst-1 (ST22-PT clone), ST1232 (CC398)-V, and ST10821 (ST8-single locus variant)-IVa. PVL-negative ST8 with SCCmec-IVl (CAMRSA/J clone, n=7) was found to harbor novel enterotoxin gene se01/sel30. As rare clones in Japan, ST5-IV (n=2) and ST5-VI (n=1) were identified in this study. This study revealed the recent clonal shift of major MRSA in northern Japan, along with the occurrence of presumptive emerging clones.
